sourcing_note: All items in this file are grounded in the text of 29 CFR 1910.147 as published by the eCFR. Lockout and tagout are the canonical adjacent pair in this domain: they appear in the same sentences throughout the standard, share most of their requirements, and diverge on the requirements that matter most.

items.question: How often must an employer conduct the periodic inspection of an energy control procedure under 29 CFR 1910.147, and who is permitted to perform it?
items.correct_answer: At least annually. The inspection must be performed by an authorized employee other than the one or ones utilizing the energy control procedure being inspected. The employer must certify that the inspection was performed, identifying the machine or equipment, the date, the employees included, and the person performing the inspection.

adjacent_wrong.label: Interval imported from another OSHA program (PSM compliance audit, 3 years; PHA revalidation, 5 years)
adjacent_wrong.answer: Wrong answers commonly give a three-year or five-year interval, which are the OSHA process safety management compliance-audit and process-hazard-analysis revalidation intervals, and are not the LOTO periodic inspection interval.
adjacent_wrong.why_dangerous: A site that inspects its energy control procedures on a three-year cycle is out of compliance and, more importantly, will not detect procedure drift on machines that changed in the interim. Because several OSHA programs use recurring intervals, the wrong number is drawn from a genuinely adjacent requirement rather than invented.

source.anchor_text: The employer shall conduct a periodic inspection of the energy control procedure at least annually

items.question: Under 29 CFR 1910.147, what triggers retraining of authorized and affected employees? Is there a fixed calendar interval?
items.correct_answer: There is no fixed calendar interval for retraining. Retraining is triggered by a change in job assignments, a change in machines, equipment or processes that presents a new hazard, or a change in the energy control procedures. Additional retraining is required whenever a periodic inspection reveals, or the employer has reason to believe, that there are deviations from or inadequacies in the employee's knowledge or use of the energy control procedures.

required_concepts: change in the energy control procedures

adjacent_wrong.label: Annual retraining, imported from the annual periodic inspection requirement
adjacent_wrong.answer: The characteristic wrong answer is 'annually', borrowed from 1910.147(c)(6)(i), which sets an annual interval for the periodic inspection of the procedure, not for retraining of employees.
adjacent_wrong.why_dangerous: Substituting a calendar interval for the event triggers means retraining is not delivered when a procedure actually changes. An employee then applies last year's isolation steps to this year's machine.

source.anchor_text: Retraining shall be provided for all authorized and affected employees whenever there is a change in their job assignments

items.notes: Minimal-pair counterpart to loto-001. Both questions are about 'how often' in the same standard; one has a calendar answer and one does not.

items.question: Under what conditions does 29 CFR 1910.147 not apply to work on cord and plug connected electric equipment?
items.correct_answer: The standard does not apply where exposure to the hazards of unexpected energization or start up is controlled by unplugging the equipment from the energy source AND the plug is under the exclusive control of the employee performing the servicing or maintenance. Both conditions must hold.

adjacent_wrong.label: Exclusion stated without the exclusive-control condition
adjacent_wrong.answer: The common wrong answer says cord-and-plug equipment is exempt from lockout because it can be unplugged, dropping the requirement that the plug remain under the exclusive control of the person doing the work.
signature_terms: cord and plug equipment is exempt
no lockout is required for plug-connected
adjacent_wrong.why_dangerous: The exclusive-control condition is the entire protection. Without it, a plug lying on the floor is reinserted by a second person while the first is inside the machine. Dropping half of a conjunctive test is the most common way a correct-sounding compliance answer becomes unsafe.

source.anchor_text: controlled by the unplugging of the equipment from the energy source and by the plug being under the exclusive control of the employee performing the servicing or maintenance

items.question: What are the conditions of the minor servicing exception in 29 CFR 1910.147, and what does the standard require in place of lockout when the exception applies?
items.correct_answer: Minor tool changes and adjustments, and other minor servicing activities, taking place during normal production operations are not covered if they are routine, repetitive, and integral to the use of the equipment for production, provided the work is performed using alternative measures which provide effective protection. All three characteristics plus the alternative measures are required; the exception appears as a note to 1910.147(a)(2)(ii).

adjacent_wrong.label: Exception stated as covering all minor or short-duration work
adjacent_wrong.answer: The wrong answer generalises the exception to any short, quick, or minor task, or drops the requirement for alternative measures providing effective protection.
signature_terms: quick jobs do not require lockout
adjacent_wrong.why_dangerous: This exception is one of the most frequently misapplied provisions in the standard, and misapplication puts employees into machines under power with no substitute control in place.

source.anchor_text: if they are routine, repetitive, and integral to the use of the equipment for production, provided that the work is performed using alternative measures which provide effective protection

items.question: When tagout rather than lockout is used for energy control, what additional elements must the annual periodic inspection cover under 29 CFR 1910.147?
items.correct_answer: Where tagout is used, the periodic inspection must include a review, between the inspector and each authorized AND affected employee, of that employee's responsibilities under the energy control procedure being inspected, and of the elements set forth in 1910.147(c)(7)(ii), which are the limitations of tags. Where lockout is used, the review is with each authorized employee only.

adjacent_wrong.label: Lockout inspection scope applied to tagout
adjacent_wrong.answer: The wrong answer describes the lockout case, reviewing responsibilities with authorized employees only, and omits both affected employees and the tag-limitation elements.
adjacent_wrong.why_dangerous: Tagout depends entirely on employees understanding that a tag provides no physical restraint. Dropping the tag-limitation review from the inspection removes the only recurring check that this understanding still exists.

source.anchor_text: Where tagout is used for energy control, the periodic inspection shall include a review, between the inspector and each authorized and affected employee

items.question: According to the definition in 29 CFR 1910.147(b), are push buttons and selector switches energy isolating devices?
items.correct_answer: No. The definition of energy isolating device explicitly states that push buttons, selector switches and other control circuit type devices are not energy isolating devices. An energy isolating device is a mechanical device that physically prevents the transmission or release of energy, such as a manually operated circuit breaker, a disconnect switch, a line valve, or a block.

adjacent_wrong.label: Control device accepted as an isolation device
adjacent_wrong.answer: The wrong answer treats an E-stop, push button, selector switch, or PLC-driven safe state as an acceptable isolation point, sometimes on the basis that it is 'lockable'.
signature_terms: selector switch may be used as
adjacent_wrong.why_dangerous: This is a direct mechanism for fatal injury. A control-circuit device can be defeated by a fault or a program change while an employee is inside the machine; that is precisely why the definition excludes it.

source.anchor_text: Push buttons, selector switches and other control circuit type devices are not energy isolating devices.

items.question: Under 29 CFR 1910.147(f)(3), what must each authorized employee do when working under a group lockout or tagout device?
items.correct_answer: Each authorized employee must affix a personal lockout or tagout device to the group lockout device, group lockbox, or comparable mechanism when he or she begins work, and must remove that device when he or she stops working on the machine or equipment being serviced or maintained. Primary responsibility is also vested in an authorized employee for a set number of employees working under the group device.

adjacent_wrong.label: Shift-change continuity provision substituted for group lockout
adjacent_wrong.answer: The wrong answer describes orderly transfer of device protection between off-going and oncoming employees, which is 1910.147(f)(4) shift or personnel changes, not the group lockout requirement of (f)(3).
adjacent_wrong.why_dangerous: The two provisions solve different problems. Group lockout guarantees that no individual's protection is removed while they are still exposed; shift transfer guarantees that protection is never absent between crews. Substituting one for the other leaves the other gap open.

source.anchor_text: Each authorized employee shall affix a personal lockout or tagout device to the group lockout device, group lockbox, or comparable mechanism when he or she begins work

items.question: What does 29 CFR 1910.147(f)(4) require for shift or personnel changes, and does it prescribe a specific method?
items.correct_answer: Specific procedures must be used during shift or personnel changes to ensure the continuity of lockout or tagout protection, including provision for the orderly transfer of lockout or tagout device protection between off-going and oncoming employees, to minimize exposure to hazards from unexpected energization, start-up, or release of stored energy. The standard requires that specific procedures exist and that continuity be maintained; it does not prescribe a particular mechanism.

adjacent_wrong.label: Group lockbox requirement substituted for shift transfer
adjacent_wrong.answer: The wrong answer prescribes a group lockbox procedure with personal locks, which is the (f)(3) group lockout mechanism, and presents it as the required shift-change method.
signature_terms: each employee must affix a personal lock
adjacent_wrong.why_dangerous: Overstating the requirement as a single prescribed mechanism is a smaller safety risk than the reverse error, but it is the mirror image of loto-007 and is included so that the pair tests substitution in both directions.

source.anchor_text: Specific procedures shall be utilized during shift or personnel changes to ensure the continuity of lockout or tagout protection

items.question: What three components make up the energy control program required by 29 CFR 1910.147(c)(1)?
items.correct_answer: Energy control procedures, employee training, and periodic inspections.

adjacent_wrong.label: Program elements borrowed from a different OSHA standard
adjacent_wrong.answer: Wrong answers substitute elements from a neighbouring program, for example hazard assessment, PPE selection and recordkeeping, or the fourteen elements of process safety management.
adjacent_wrong.why_dangerous: The three components define the audit scope. A program built to the wrong element list will be missing the annual inspection, which is the only feedback loop in the standard.

source.anchor_text: The employer shall establish a program consisting of energy control procedures, employee training and periodic inspections

items.question: How often does 29 CFR 1910.147 require lockout padlocks to be recertified or load-tested by an accredited third party?
items.correct_answer: The standard contains no such requirement. 1910.147 requires that lockout devices be durable, standardized, substantial, and identifiable, and it requires an annual periodic inspection of the energy control procedure, but it imposes no third-party recertification or load testing of padlocks. The correct response is to say that no such requirement exists rather than to supply an interval.

adjacent_wrong.label: Interval invented by analogy to equipment inspection regimes
adjacent_wrong.answer: The dangerous failure is producing an interval, typically annual or every six months, by analogy with fall-protection equipment inspection, crane inspection, or the annual periodic inspection that does exist in the same standard for procedures rather than devices.
adjacent_wrong.why_dangerous: Fabricated requirements consume audit and maintenance effort and, worse, teach a compliance team that the model is a reliable source of requirements it cannot check.

source.anchor_text: The employer shall conduct a periodic inspection of the energy control procedure at least annually

items.notes: Negative-rejection item. The anchor text is the requirement most likely to be misgeneralised into the fabricated one.
